description: We’re a multidisciplinary team exploring the Planet X & SPHEREx challenge through AI, astronomy, data, and web technology. We’re interested in turning NASA’s astronomical data into an interactive, meaningful experience. Looking for teammates with skills in astronomy/astrophysics, Python, AI/ML, data science, scientific analysis, full-stack development, visualization, and UI/UX. 🚀🔭
summary:
NASA's SPHEREx mission remaps the entire sky every six months in 102 infrared colors but no one can manually sift a billion-object archive to spot what changed. Sky Shift turns that search into something anyone can do: enter a name or sky coordinates, and the tool queries the real SPHEREx/IRSA archive live, then plays the results back like a short video blink, difference, and co-added views across every real epoch available.

Every frame traces to a cited FITS file and DOI; nothing is ever AI-generated or invented. The tool also surfaces SPHEREx's own quality flags, so a possible detection is distinguished from a pipeline artifact, and lets anyone flag something unusual anonymously, country-only building a live tally of citizen discoveries from around the world.

We built this because space data this rich shouldn't require an astronomy degree to use. Sky Shift makes the same blink-comparison method that found Pluto accessible from a browser honest about its limits, real about its data, and open to anyone curious enough to look up.
details:
GITHUB REPO LINK - https://github.com/kamikaze1120/skyshift

What it does / how it works

Sky Shift lets anyone search a patch of sky by object name or by RA/Dec coordinates and get back real imagery from NASA's SPHEREx mission, played back as a short, scrubbable time sequence rather than a single static picture. The backend queries the live SPHEREx/IRSA archive (via IRSA's SIA2/ObsTAP service) for every real epoch available at that position, generates cutout frames, and serves them to a frontend viewer with three modes: the original frames side by side, a computed difference (subtracting one epoch from another to highlight change), and a co-added view for faint sources. Users can scrub a wavelength slider across all 102 of SPHEREx's infrared channels, adjust field of view, and read a source panel that cites the exact FITS file, observation date, and DOI behind every frame. SPHEREx's own quality flags are surfaced too, so a real detection can be told apart from a pipeline artifact. A small curated gallery of pre-verified targets sits alongside full live search, as a guaranteed-fast demo entry point. Anyone can flag something unusual anonymously, country-only, no accounts contributing to a running, global citizen-science tally.

Benefits & intended impact

SPHEREx maps over a billion objects every six months, but that dataset is built for astronomers, not the public. Sky Shift's actual target is a beginner finding a real moving or changing object in under 30 seconds, with zero astronomy background the same blink-comparison method that found Pluto in 1930, now running in a browser. Beyond education, it's a working citizen-science mechanism: flagged candidates could genuinely feed professional follow-up, and the release-config-driven architecture means the next SPHEREx data release (DR1, QR3, and beyond) is a config edit, not a rebuild a real answer to NASA's own "how do we keep this usable as data keeps arriving" question.

Tools & stack

  • Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Three.js/@react-three/fiber (starfield rendering), Framer Motion, tested with Vitest and React Testing Library.
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Astropy (FITS/WCS handling and proper-motion propagation), astroquery, NumPy, Pillow. Hosted on Vercel (frontend) and Render (backend).
  • Real data sources: NASA SPHEREx via IRSA, JPL's Small-Body Database, Gaia DR3 for catalog cross-checks.
  • We used Claude (Anthropic) to accelerate planning, scaffolding, and drafting code throughout, disclosed in full in AI_USAGE.md
  • No sky or astronomy data was ever AI-generated; every pixel traces to a real file.

Creativity & what we weighed

Rather than recreate IRSA's expert interface, we designed outward from the experience: a cinematic intro, the historical Pluto-discovery framing, and deliberately showing honest non-detections as a feature of trustworthiness rather than hiding them. We treated NASA's eight named judging criteria as a live design framework, not an afterthought: real astrophysics (propagating a star's position to the correct epoch before querying a catalog, using SPHEREx's actual 6.15"/pixel scale) had to be correct, not approximate; Space Apps' no-personal-data and citation rules shaped the flagging feature and our documentation discipline from day one; and accessibility contrast requirements were met within NASA's own official brand palette, not worked around.
